note: Sunday weekend run, 27 Sep 2026 07:02 SGT. All cash markets remain closed since Fri 25 Sep US close (S&P +0.51% to 7,743.41, Nasdaq +0.48% to 27,068.72, Dow +0.93% to 51,828.62, VIX ~14.87; 10-year Treasury yield 5.18%, highest since 2008) -- no new session has traded, so Friday's OHLC stands, but the geopolitical setup underneath it moved materially over the weekend. On Saturday 26 Sep Trump publicly rejected Iran's formal seven-day Hormuz-reopening roadmap (submitted via Qatar Fri 25 Sep), calling it 'not acceptable' and telling aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November US midterms; a separately planned Iran-Gulf-states meeting on Hormuz terms was also postponed over the weekend. Iran's FM Araghchi said Sunday 27 Sep that Tehran is still awaiting a 'formal' US response and has not declared the ~Mon-Tue 28-29 Sep ultimatum deadline void, but the truce-hope framing that eased oil Friday has clearly reversed: oil futures gapped higher into the Sunday Globex reopen (Brent back toward ~$103, WTI ~$97, both up ~1.5-2% from Friday's close) on report of the rejection. Bitcoin, the only market trading through the weekend, fell ~3.8% to ~$83,900 immediately on the rejection headline before recovering to ~$84,000; crypto-wide liquidations hit ~$255M Sat. Fear & Greed held flat at 37/Fear (checked Sunday, no new reading). No new BofA Flow Show regional/gold/money-market sub-split for the week ended 23 Sep has surfaced. The coming week's key data point is the 2 Oct nonfarm payrolls report (consensus roughly halving to ~85k from August's 162k) alongside a heavy Fed-speaker calendar and KRX reopening Mon 28 Sep after the 4-day Chuseok closure. Net effect: the regime holds ('Hawkish-Fed war-shock') but the Iran leg has shifted from 'two-sided, truce-hope' toward 'escalation more likely into the deadline, resolution deferred past the midterms' -- riskOnProb nudged down modestly to reflect that, and the XLE/USO/GLD/SLV drivers below are updated for the weekend oil reversal.

macro.regime: Hawkish-Fed war-shock: Iran escalation risk rising into the deadline
macro.narrative: The regime holds -- hawkish Fed, stressed rates, live war-shock -- but the Iran leg moved from 'two-sided, truce-hope' to 'escalation more likely' over the weekend, nudging riskOnProb down modestly from Friday's 0.55. Equities rallied into Friday's close (S&P +0.51% to 7,743.41, Dow snapping a 3-week losing streak) even as the 10-year Treasury yield pushed to 5.18% -- its highest since the 2008 financial crisis -- a divergence BlackRock's Rick Rieder called 'not a crisis but an eye-opener,' and the BofA Flow Show (week ended 23 Sep) showed fund flows reversing sharply (US equity funds -$21.1bn versus +$63.8bn the prior week). Then on Saturday 26 Sep, Trump publicly rejected Iran's formal seven-day Hormuz-reopening roadmap (submitted via Qatar Fri 25 Sep) as 'not acceptable,' telling aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms -- a materially harder line than Friday's truce-hope framing that had eased Brent to ~$105.3. A separate Iran-Gulf-states meeting on Hormuz terms was also postponed over the weekend. Iran's FM Araghchi said Sunday the regime is still awaiting a 'formal' US response and has not declared its ~Mon-Tue 28-29 Sep ultimatum deadline void, but oil futures already gapped higher into the Sunday Globex reopen (Brent back toward ~$103, WTI ~$97) on the rejection headline, and Bitcoin -- the only market trading through the weekend -- fell ~3.8% before partly recovering. Gold and silver extended Friday's pullback on the firmer dollar/higher-real-yield backdrop, but the weekend's renewed war premium is a fresh, partially offsetting tailwind into Monday -- not yet reflected in Friday's OHLC. This week's Trump-Xi Washington summit held the China trade truce at status quo with no new rare-earth concessions (Aug US-bound magnet shipments still -21% MoM). The week ahead's dominant scheduled catalyst is the 2 Oct nonfarm payrolls report (consensus roughly halving to ~85k from 162k), which will test whether the Fed's hawkish path holds. Credit spreads remain historically tight, leaving little cushion if the Iran deadline lapses without a deal or payrolls surprise either direction.
